Thursday, the 26th April, 2007/6 Vaisakha, 1929 (Saka)                                                                             
The House met at eleven of the clock, 
MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair. 
MEMBER SWORN 
Prof. M.S. Swaminathan (Nominated) 
OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound s orrow to the 
passing away of Shri Sawaisingh Sisodia, a former Member of this House, on the 
24th March, 2007, at the age of 88 years. 
Born at Barnagar in the Ujjain district of Madhya Pradesh in November, 1919, 
Shri Sisodia had his education at Madhav College, U jjain and Law College, 
Bombay. 
An Advocate and a social worker, Shri Sisodia was a ssociated with 
various social welfare, educational and financial organizations and served them in 
different capacities. He worked for the upliftment of backward classes and 
took keen interest in the promotion of co-operative movement, agricultural work 
and cultural activities. 
Shri Sisodia was Chairman of the Children's Education Society, Ujjain, State 
Co-operative Union of Madhya Pradesh and Vice-Chair man of the National 
Co-operative Union of India. He also served as Director of the Indian Farmers 
Fertilizer Co-operatives Ltd. 
The legislative career of Shri Sisodia started with  the membership of the 
erstwhile Madhya Bharat Legislative Assembly, where he was a Member from 1952 
to 1956. He was also a member of the Madhya Pradesh  Legislative Assembly 
from 1956-1957. He served as Deputy Minister and 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
Minister in the Governments of Madhya Bharat and Madhya Pradesh from 
1952 to 1957. 
Shri Sisodia represented the State of Madhya Pradesh in this House fofthree 
terms, from April 1969toApril 1970; April 1970toApr il 1976 and again from 
April 1976 to April 1982. He was Chairman of the Ho use Committee, Rajya 
Sabha, from April to October 1980. 
Shri Sisodia had the distinction of serving as Union Minister of State in the 
Ministry of Finance in 1980. 
In the passing away of Shri Sawaisingh Sisodia the country has lost a 
devoted social worker, an able administrator and a distinguished 
Parliamentarian. 
I request Members to rise in their places and obser ve silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
Re: Demand for postponement of Question Hour  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy. 
...(Interruptions)....  
REFERENCES BY THE CHAIR 
To The Victims of Terrorist Attacks in Algiers and Casablanca 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, this House expresses its shock and grief 
over the terrorist attacks in Algiers on the 11th A pril, 2007 which resulted in 
the death of more than 30 civilans and injuries to more than 160 persons. The 
attacks on the Office of the Prime Minister and the  Interior Minister of the 
Government of People's Democratic Republic of Alger ia, is downright 
deplorable. 
This House strongly condemns these attack on innoce nt civilians and the 
structures of governance. It places on record its d eep condolences to the 
bereaved families. 
This House reiterates the solidarity of the people of India with their 
Algerian brethren in their common struggle against the menace of global 
terrorism. 
2 

[26 April, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Hon. Members, this House also expresses its shock and grief over the recent 
terrorist related incidents in Casablanca in April 2007 aimed at the civilian 
population and at disrupting peace. 
This House reiterates the solidarity of the pople o f India with their 
Morocqan brethren in their common struggle against the menace of 
terriorism. 
The scourge of terrorism cannot be condoned in any form, or under any guise or 
motivation, and must be confronted with determination and firmness. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark respect 
to the memory of those who lost their lives in these tragedies. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
Re.: Demand for postponement of Question Hour

Criteria for identification of BPL people 
*341. SHRI A. VIJAYRAGHAVAN: Will the PRIME MINISTE R be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the criteria adopted to identify the people Below Poverty Line; 
(b) whether it is a uniform in all the States; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details of parameters in different States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The identification of  People Below 
Poverty Line in rural areas is done through census with 100% coverage in each 
village. Thirteen scorable indicators are assigned scrores (0,1,2,3,4) and then total 
score for each household is calculated. The thirteen indicators are: 
1. Size group of operational holding of land, 
2. Type of house, 
3. Average availability of normal wear clothing (per person in pieces), 
5 

 RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
4. Food Security, 
5. Sanitation, 
6. Ownership of consumer durables, 
7. Literacy status of the highest literate adult, 
8. Status of the Household Labour Force, 
9. Means of livelihood, 
10. Status of children (5-14 years), 
11. Type of indebtedness, 
12. Reason for migration from household and 
13. Preference of assistance. 
The States/UTs may exercise flexibility to decide the cut-off scores for identifying and 
categorizing of the households into "Poor" and "Non-Poor". The cut-off scores may be 
decided after tabulating the data for the entire State. 
To identify the BPL families, a census is carried out every five years by the Ministry of 
Rural development with the help of State Governments. The States/UTs may identify the 
BPL households for targeting under different programmes of the Government in such a way 
that total number of persons identified in the State/UT does not exceed the number of 
persons living Below the Poverty Line in that State, estimated by the Planning 
Commission. 
(b) The methodology of survey is uniform throughout the country, and the same 13 
criteria are used by all States. However, the cut-off score below which a family is 
considered "poor" is likely to vary from State to State. This is because the total number of 
persons identified in the State/ UT should not exceed the number of BPL persons in that State, as 
estimated by the Planning Commission. 
(c) and (d) Do not arise. 
6

Ascertaining people living Below Poverty Line 
 †342. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD:  
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 'Uniform Recall Period' a nd 'Mixed Recall 
Period' systems are used to ascertain the number of  people living below the 
poverty line; 
(b) if so, the facts thereof and in what way the calcul ation is made under 
the systems; and 
(c) the assesment of the income of poor people under bo th the systems at 
present? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) The Planning Commission estimates the 
incidence of poverty at national and State level from the large sample survey on 
household consumer expenditure conducted by the Nat ional Sample Survey 
Organization (NSSO) at an interval of approximately five years following the 
methodology contained in the Report of the Expert G roup on Estimation of 
Proportion and number of Poor (Lakadwala Committee). 
On the basis of the latest large sample survey data  on household consumer 
expenditure (61 st Round of NSS), covering the period July, 2004 to June, 2005 
[Report No. 508 (6171.0/1)], two different consumpt ion distributions for the 
year 2004-05 have been obtained. The first one from  the consumption data 
collected using 30-day recall period (also known as reference period) for all the 
items. The other distribution is obtained from the consumer expenditure data 
collected using 365-day recall period for five infrequently purchased non-food 
items, namely, clothing, footwear, durable goods, e ducation and institutional 
medical expenses and 30-day recall period for the remaining items,. These two 
consumption distributions have been termed as Unifo rm Recall Period (URP) 
consumption distribution and Mixed Recall Period (M RP) consumption 
distribution respectively. The Planning Commission,  using the Expert Group 
methodology has estimated poverty in 2004-05 using both the distributions. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
The URP-consumption distribution data of the 61st Round yields a poverty ratio 
of 28.3 per cent in the rural areas, 25.7 per cent in the urban areas and 27.5 per cent 
for the country as a whole in 2004-05. The corresponding figures obtained from 
the MRP-consumption distribution data of the 61st Round are 21.8 per cent in the 
rural areas, 21.7 per cent in the urban areas and 21.8 per cent for the country as a 
whole. 
(c) The data on income of the poor people are not available. However, per capita 
consumption expenditure of the poor estimated for the year 2004-05 (based on NSS 
61st Round of consumption expenditure data) is Rs. 286.10 per capita per month in the 
rural areas and Rs. 416.15 per capita per month in the urban areas as per URP consumption 
distribution, and Rs. 325.40 per capita per month in the rural areas and Rs. 467.90 per 
capita per month in the urban areas, as per MRP consumption distribution.

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
April 3-4,2007 adopted a comprehensive and a forward-looking Declaration, to 
promote regional co-operation. It underlined the collective vision of the Heads of 
State/Government of SAARC countries of an interconnected South Asia where there 
was a free flow of people, goods, services and idea s. Based on the region's 
common history, geography and socio-cultural ties, it reiterated that the future of 
the people of South Asia was interlinked. When impl emented, the decisions 
outlined in the Declaration will boost intra-region al trade and investment, 
enhance understanding through increased people-to-people contact and promote 
cultural exchanges and travel within the region. 
2. The salient features of the Declaration of the Fourteenth Meeting Of the Heads 
of State or Government adopted at the Kew Delhi SAARC Summit are: 
• In its third decade of existence, there was a need to move SAARC from a 
declaratory to an implementation phase. The focus of SAARC should be on 
implementing collaborative projects that would bring concrete benefits to 
the people of the region. In this context, SAARC co untries committed 
themselves to early operationalisation of the SAARC  Development 
Fund (SDF). 
• It was agreed to improve intra-regional connectivit y, particularly 
physical, economic and people-to-people connectivity. 
• The full benefits of an integrated regional multi-modal transport 
- system were recognised. It was agreed that the SAARC Regional 
Multimodal Transport Study would be extended to Afghanisthan. It was 
also agreed that pilot projects for improving conne ctivity be identified 
and implemented. 
• The signing of two important Agreements on the esta blishment of the 
South Asian University and the SAARC Food Bank was welcomed. 
• The SAARC countries agreed to work together on a roadmap, inter alia, in 
the fields of poverty alleviation, food security, energy, water, environment, 
climate change, trade and transport, information an d communication 
technology, tourism, education, culture and counter-terrorism. 
• The Agreement on South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA ) should be 
implemented in letter and spirit. To realise its full potential, SAFTA 
10 

[26 April, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
should integrate trade in services. The importance of implementing trade 
facilitation measures was also underlined. 
• The importance of people-to-people contact as a key  constituent in 
regional connectivity was stressed. 
• The SAARC countries committed themselves to combat terrorism and 
agreed to consider India's proposal to work towards  finalizing an 
Agreement on Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters. 
3. Bilateral and contentious issues are explicitly excluded by the SAARC 
Charter from SAARC's deliberations. Implementation of the Declaration will 
considerably upgrade regional cooperation and positively impact on the climate 
of relations in the subcontinent as a whole.

*355. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the PRIME MINIST ER be 
pleased  to state: 
20 

[26 April, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
       (a) whether the focus of economic planning over next five years Would be on 
the ways and means to faster inclusive growth in the economy 
(b) if so, the objective to bring a policy change that ensures a four per cent 
growth in agriculture is on the agenda; 
(c) how the projected growth rate of four per cent in agriculture is expected to be 
achieved and what measures at the ground level enco mpassing rainfed and 
irrigated areas would be implemented; 
 
(d) whether poultry, fisheries, horticulture, sericultu re and animal 
husbandry would be given the allied sector status and whether all credit facilities, 
given to agriculture would be extended to the allied sectors; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) to (c) The Approach Paper for the 11th Five 
Year Plan envisages restructuring of policies to achieve a new vision based on 
faster, more broad-based and inclusive growth in th e economy as focus of 
economic planning over the next five years. Agricul ture sector still provides 
livelihood to nearly 60 per cent of our people and remains vital for food security. To 
ensure a better life for women and men engaged in agriculture, it is necessary to 
double the growth rate achieved in 10th Plan and put agriculture on a growth path of 
around 4 per cent per annum. To do this and at the same time maintain prices and 
profitability, a corresponding increase in demand for agricultural output matched 
with the supply side response based on productivity improvements is required. 
The 11th Plan strategy to raise agricultural output, as reflected in the Approach 
Paper, emphasizes on the following elements:— 
— Double the rate of growth of irrigated area; 
— Improve water management, rain water harvesting and  watershed 
development; 
— Reclaim degraded land and focus on soil quality; 
— Bridge the knowledge gap through effective extension; 
— Diversify into high value outputs, fruits, vegetables, flowers, herbs and 
spices, medicinal plants, bamboo,87 bio-diesel etc., but with adequate 
measures to ensure food security; 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
— Promote animal husbandry and fishery; 
— Provide easy access to credit at affordable rates; 
— Improve the incentive structure and functioning of markets; 
— Refocus on land reforms issues; 
— Energize the National Agricultural Research System and improve its 
capacity to develop and deliver innovative and effe ctive technologies 
relevant to the current contexts and needs. 
(d) to (e) Poultry, fisheries, sericulture and anim al husbandry have been 
classified under allied sector and horticulture under Primary Sector. There has 
been steady increase in credit to agriculture, including its allied sectors, in recent 
years. Since the announcement of 'Farm Credit Packa ge' in June 2004, 
stipulating doubling of the flow of institutional credit for agriculture in the ensuing 
three years, the overal agricultural lending by all  agencies (i.e. Commercial 
Banks, Regional Rural Banks and Co-operative Banks) has increased from Rs. 
86,981 crore in 2003-04 to Rs. 1,80,486 crore in 2005-06.

*357. SHRI PENUMALLI MADHU: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the mandatory reforms proposed in the Jawaharlal Nehru -. 
National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM); 
26 

[26 April, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether they are being conditioned by World 3ank loans; 
(c) whether the user charges are part of mandatory reforms; and 
(d) whether taxes collected by local bodies are intende d to meet the 
services, collecting user charges? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI AJAY MAKEN): (a) Details of the m andatory 
reforms are as under:— 
There are two sets of mandatory reforms. Core reforms at ULB/Parastatal level 
aim at process re-engineering through deployment of technology to enable more 
efficient, reliable, timely services in a transpare nt manner. The other set of 
reforms are framework related at the State level. 
URBAN LOCAL BODY/PARASTATAL LEVEL REFORMS: 
i. Adoption of modern, accrual-based double entry s ystem of accounting 
in Urban Local Bodtes/Parastatals. 
ii. Introduction of system of e-governance using IT applications like, GIS 
and MIS for various services provided by ULBs/Parastatals. 
Hi. Reform of property tax with GIS, so that it bec omes major source of 
revenue for Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and arrangements for its effective 
implementation so that collection efficiency reache s at least 85% 
within next seven years. 
iv. Levy of reasonable user charges by ULBs/Parastatals with the objective 
that full cost of operation and maintenance or recurring cost is collected 
within next seven years. However, cities/towns in North East and other 
special catrgory States may recover at least 50% of  operation and 
maintenance charges initially. These cities/ towns should graduate to full 
O and M cost recovery in a phased manner. 
v. Internal earmarking within local body budgets for basic services to the 
urban poor. 
vi. Provision of basic services to urban poor including security of tenure at 
affordable prices, improved housing, water supply, sanitation and ensuring 
delivery of other - already existing universal services of the Government for 
education, health and social security. 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
STATE LEVEL REFORMS: 
i. Implementation of decentralization measures as e nvisaged in 74th 
Constitution Amendment Act. The States should ensur e meaningful 
association/engagement of ULBs in planning function of parastatals as well 
as delivery of services to the citizens. 
ii.  Repeal of Urban Land Ceiling and Regulation Act. 
iii. 'Reform of Rent Control Laws balancing the int erests of landlords and 
tenants. 
iv. Rationalisation of Stamp Duty to bring it down to no more than 5% 
within next seven years. 
v. Enactment of Public Disclosure Law to ensure pre paration of medium-
term ffscal plan of ULBs/Parastatals and release of quarterly performance 
information to all stakeholders. 
vi. Enactment of Community Participation Law to ins titutionalize citizen 
participation and introducing the concept of Area Sabha in urban areas. 
vii. Assigning or associating elected ULBs with "city planning function". Over 
a period of seven years, transferring all special agencies that deliver civic 
services in urban areas to ULBs and creating accoun tability platforms 
for all urban civic service providers in transition. 
(b) No, Sir. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir.

Atomic energy target set for 2020  
2573. SHRI VIJAYKUMAR RUPANI: Will the PRIME MINIST ER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the target set for atomic energy production in vision 2020 looking to the 
potential of atomic energy of the country; 
(b) the total production of atomic energy as on 31.12.2 006 as against the 
target of 5000 MW in the year 2000; 
(c) the plans of Nuclear Power Corporation and National  Thermal Power 
Corporation to reach the target set for 2020; and 
(d) whether it is a fact that some environmentalists ar e opposing the 
establishment of Atomic Power Plants in the country; 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE (SHRI 
PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) the document "Long Term vision of Department of 
Atomic Energy -Vision 2020" envisages reaching a total installed nuclear power 
capacity of 20,000 MWe by the year 2020. 
(b) the document envisaged reaching a total nuclear power capacity of 3260 
MWe by December 2006. The actual achievement in this regard has been 3900 
MWe. 
(c) Kaiga-3 (220 MWe) has been synchronized to the grid  on 11th April 
2007 and the total nuclear power capacity as on date is 4120 MWe. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
Six nuclear power reactors of total capacity of 316 0 MWe being constructed 
by NPCIL and BHAVINI are in advanced stages of cons truction and the total 
nuclear power capacity will reach 7280 MWe progressively by the end of XI 
plan. 
The XI Plan proposals envisage commencement of work  of 8 indigenous 
reactors with a total capacity of 5600 MWe by NPCIL . Additions of Fast 
Breeder Reactors built indigenously and import of L ight Water Reactors 
through imports, depending on the opening of intern ational civil nuclear 
cooperation, will take the power generation capacity further. 
(d) While the public opinion in the country about nuclear power is generally 
favourable, some activists/NGOs/environmentalists have been expressing location 
specific concerns, which are addressed suitably by the Government on case by case 
basis. 
Disposal of atomic energy waste 
2574. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a)the places where the waste of atomic energy of vari ous plants in India 
disposed of; 
(b) the details thereof, plant-wise and area-wise; 
(c) the quantity of atomic energy waste produced annually in India; 
(d) whether any study has so far been undertaken on the  ill-effects of the 
waste of atomic energy in India; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE (SHRI 
PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) to (c) Wastes generated at the Nuclear Power 
Stations during their operation are of low and inte rmediate activity level and 
are managed at the site itself. These wastes are tr eated, concentrated and 
immobilized in solid matrices like cement, bitumen,  polymers etc. and stored 
in specially constructed structures such as reinforced concrete trenches and tile 
holes, located at each site. The amount of waste is  about 100 cubic meters per 
year at each station. 
40 

[26 April, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
There are also facilities for Research and Development (R&D) in various aspects 
of isotope production and their application etc. located at Trombay. Mainly low and 
intermediate level wastes are produced in these facilities. These are also stored at 
specially designed near surface underground structu res similar to those at 
nuclear power plants. 
Besides low level & intermediate level wastes, the high level radioactive wastes 
are also produced in the spent fuel reprocessing plant. These are immobilised in 
vitrious matrix and doubly encapsulated. Solid wast e so conditioned is stored 
in air cooled engineered vault facility located ins ide the boundaries of the 
installation at Tarapur. The sites where multiple nuclear activities such as R&D, fuel 
fabrication and fuel reprocessing, are carried out (at Trombay, Tarapur and 
Kalpakkam), about 400 - 600 cubic meter of radioactive solid waste is disposed 
annually. 
(d) and (e) Extensive study is performed on a given  site before design, 
construction and commissioning of a waste disposal facility. This study 
includes ground water movement, soil and water analysis, water table, surface 
water movement, etc. The radioactive waste disposal  system uses a multi 
barrier concept comprising of waste form/matrix, en gineered barrier, backfill 
material and the natural geo-environment to contain and isolate the radioactivity 
from the environment. The performance of disposal facility is monitored through 
a systematic surveillance programme consisting of s ystematic ground 
water/soil analysis for radioactivity as well as ra diation monitoring of the 
disposal area. No ill effect has been observed eith er because of the facility or 
because of waste disposal at the facility. 
(f) No applicable.

Indians with forged documents in Spain  
†2634. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRI SATYAVRAT CHATURVEDI: 
Will the Minister of OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that a group of 150 Indians was sent to Spain on 
forged documents by a travel agency in February and April, 2006; 
(b) whether it is a fact that whereabouts of this group of Indians are still not 
known; 
(c) the action taken by Government to find out the lost Indians; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that some other travel ag encies are also sending 
Indians abroad on forged documents; and 
(e) if so, the steps taken by Government to identif y the guilty travel 
agencies and take action against them? 
THE MINISTER OF OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS (SHRI VAYAL AR 
RAVI): (a) to (c) As per the information received f rom Indian Mission in 
Madrid, Spain, there have been reports in the media that a group of Punjabi youth 
went missing on their way to Spain. They were purpo rtedly travelling on 
"incentive trips" arranged by a tour operator namely Tanvir Tours and Travels, 
who claimed that the trip was organised by Hero Cyc le, an Indian cycle 
manufacturer. Spanish Embassy in New Delhi has filed an FIR with theTughlaq 
Road Police Station regarding forged Spanish Visas on which this group 
travelled. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
112 

[26 April, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) As per the information available the journey of ill egal immigrants is 
arranged by some unscrupulous agents but the immigrants do not divulge details 
of these agents. However, as far as ECR countries a re concerned, a few cases 
have come to the notice of the Ministry from time t o time where the workers 
have been" sent abroad by illegal/unscrupulous Recruiting agents. 
(e) In case of such activities by unregistered Recruiting Agents, State Police 
is requested to take legal action-. Concerned POE also files FIR. 
During the last three years 2004 to 2006 about 170 complaints have been 
filed against the unregistered recruiting agents and 38 (including 21 alone in 
2006) prosecution sanctions issued. 
In respect of such complaints against any registered Recruiting agent, action 
like show cause, suspension, cancellation of certif icate and even forfeiture of 
Bank Guarantee is taken. In appropriate cases, FIR is also filed. During the last 
two years 2005-2006 about 52 registration certificates were cancelled. 
HSMP programme of UK  
  2635. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether, faced with an uncertain future, about 30,000 Indians who went to 
London for looking better prospects under the Highly Skilled Migrants Progamme 
have appealed to the President and Prime Minister to take up their plight with the 
British Prime Minister to ensure that new migrants rules were not made 
applicable to those who are already in the UK under the HSMP; 
(b) whether the British Government have victimized by c hanging the rules 
of the Highly Skilled Migrants Programme under which they went there; and 
(c) if so, to what extent Government have agreed to consider their request? 
THE MINISTER OF OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS (SHRI VAYALAR 
RAVI): (a) The UK Home Office, in March, 2006, presented to the Parliament 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
with the new immigration guidelines "A Point-based System : Making 
Migration Work for Britain" and announced its imple mentation from 7th 
November, 2006. According to the new guidelines, for an extension of visa or for 
Indefinite Leave of Settlement, a person staying in the UK under HSMP has to 
earn 75 points. The revised rules require the appli cants to re-qualify through a 
stringent points based system on the basis of his age, earnings and UK experience 
for their further visa extension as against economi c activity alone when 
entered into the UK. 
(b) and (c) The new HSMP rules are applicable to pr ofessionals from all 
countries who have migrated to the UK under the Programme. It is expected that the 
majority of migrants currently in the UK under the HSMP will qualify under 
the new point-based system. It has been informed by  the Government of UK 
that transitional arrangements have been put in place to support those existing 
participants of the HSMP who will fail to satisfy t he new points scoring 
assessment. The HSMP is designed to attract only highly skilled young people 
to the UK to seek and take work.

House during Winter Session 2006. A brief summary is outlined below: 
1. The Ministry of Panchayati Raj is an innovation of the UPA Government 
because no previous government has had a separate Ministry or even

[26 April, 2007] RAJYA SABHA 
Department of Panchayati Raj. The Ministry of Panch ayati Raj came into 
existence on 27th May, 2004, and within a month, Hon'ble Prime Minister called 
his very first Conference of Chief Ministers on 24th June 2004, on the subject 
"Rural Prosperity and Poverty Eradication through P anchayati Raj". While 
inaugurating the Conference, he spoke of Panchayati Raj being a medium to 
transform rural India into 700 million opportunities, of Gram Swaraj being the 
key instrument for integrating economic reforms wit h institutional reforms in 
the country side, the challenges of institutionaliz ing the system of local self-
governance while also making it the world's most representative and participatory 
democracy. The first mandate of the Ministry of Pan chayati Raj is to ensure 
conformity to the Constitutional provisions of Part IX of the Constitution read with 
Article 243 ZD of Part IXA relating to the District Planning Committees together 
with the Eleventh Schedule which sets out a list of 29 matters, to be considered 
by State Legislatures for devolution to the Panchayats. While the Ministry of 
Panchayati Raj must ensure conformity to these Cons titutional provisions, the 
Constitution of India charges the States (not the Centre) with the responsibility 
for devolution. In other words, the processes and c ontent of devolution of 
functions, finances and functionaries — the crux of Power to the Panchayats — are 
vested entirely in State Legislatures', reinforcing  the inclusion of Panchayati 
Raj in the State List of the Seventh Schedule. 
2. The first task before the Ministry was to evolve a national consensus in 
respect of the Roadmap for Panchayati Raj through mutual consultation between 
the Centre and the States. Ministry of Panchayati Raj convened Seven Round 
Tables of State Panchayati Raj Ministers with the U nion Minister of 
Panchayati Raj between July and December 2004. The deliberations centered 
on the 18 identified dimensions of Panchayati Raj r anging from the effective 
Devolution of the Functions, Finances and Functiona ries to District Planning, 
Training and Capacity Building and IT-enabled e-govemance. At the conclusion 
of each Round Table, nearly 150 action points comprised in the Compendium 
were unanimously adopted by all Panchayati Raj Ministers and referred to State 
Governments/UTs for taking necessary action. This h as become a National 
Roadmap for effective Panchayati Raj. 
3. A Committee of Panchayati Raj Secretaries was constituted to monitor the 
progress and implementation of these 150 Action Poi nts. This Committee of 
Secretaries headed by the Secretary, Ministry of Panchayati

(a) whether Government are aware that Deputy  Chairman of the Planning Commission is

Commission of Growth and Development of World Bank and the Institute of 
International Finance;

member of the World Bank while Indian institutions are members of the

Views regarding Indian economy 
    †2663. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD:                             
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently several renowned economists have expressed their 
views that Indian economy is witnessing overheating i.e. an artificail monentary 
development; 
(b) if so, the facts thereof and on what basis these economists have expressed their 
said views; and 
(c) Government's reaction regarding the said views? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI M.V. 
RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The macro and monetary management are carried out by the 
Ministry of Finance and Reserve Bank of India who monitor development on a regular 
basis and take appropriate monetary and other policy measures. Some have expressed a 
view that there are signs of overheating in the Indian economy and the nine per cent rate of 
economic growth putting pressure on inflation. The concern for a possible "overheating" of 
the Indian economy has risen with the rate of economic growth scaling to 9 per cent in the 
past two years, and accompanying an inflation rate of five per cent plus. 
(c) The Government (i.e., the Finance Ministry, in particular) and the monetary 
establishment (i.e., the Reserve Bank of India) have responded to the price inflation in 
critical areas of the economy through a slew of fiscal and monetary measures, which 
include increase in interest rates, reduction in import duty rates, ban on exports of certain 
items and a ban on fitures trading in certain agricultural commodities.

(b) The Planning Commission uses a poverty line based o n per capita 
consumption, expenditure as the criterion to. determine the percentage of persons 
living below the poverty line. The per capita consumption norm at the national 
level has been fixed at Rs. 49.09 per month in the rural areas and Rs. 56.64 per 
month in the urban areas at 1973-74 prices corresponding to a basket of goods and 
services anchored on a norm of per capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 koal 
in the. rural areas and 2100 koal in the urban areas. These national level poverty 
lines in the rural and urban areas are disaggregated into State-specific poverty 
lines using State-specific price indices and inter- State price differentials. These 
State-specific poverty lines of 1973-74 pre updated for the later years using 
State-specific Consumer Price Index of Agricultural Labourers (CPIAL) in the 
rural areas and Consumer Price Index of Industrial Workers (CPllW) in the 
urban areas following the methodology contained in the Report of the Expert 
Group of Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor, The latest estimate of 
State-wise poverty lines is available for the year 2004-05. These are given in

2667. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Prime Minister outlined five areas i .e. revitalization of rural 
economy, improved delivery of public services, improved management of urban 
areas, making our financial system more inclusive a longwith being globally 
integrated and putting in place a viable regulator/ framework that ensures cost 
effective investment in the infrastructure; and

the next ten years?

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI M. 
V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The Prime Minister in an addr ess at the Golden 
Jubilee Celebrations of the National Council of App lied Economic Research 
(NCAER) in December 2006 emphasized five challenges  to engage the 
country over the next decade. These are: (i) revitalisation of the rural economy, 
(ii) improved delivery of essential public services, (iii) improved management of 
urban areas, (iv) preparing financial system for greater inclusion and increased 
global integration and (v) establishing a regulator y culture to facilitate cost-
effective private investment in infrastructure. 
(b) For the rural economy the Approach Paper to the  Eleventh Five Year 
Plan aims at achieving a growth rate of 4% in agriculture sector For that there is a 
focus on improving rural connectivity, scaling up of irrigation potential creation, 
watershed management, rainwater harvesting and grou nd water recharge, 
revitalizatjon of the extension system which links universities and best practices 
to farmers, etc. The Accelerated Irrigation Benefit  Programme (AIBP) and 
Accelerated Power Development Reform Programme (APD RP) are being 
implemented to augment irrigation and power, respec tively. Bharat Nirman is 
a time-bound business plan for action in rural infr astructure over the four-year 
period (2005-2009). Under Bharat Nirman, action is proposed in the areas of 
irrigation, rural roads, rural housing, rural water  supply, rural electrification 
and rural telecommunication connectivity. The Jawah arlal Nehru National 
Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) has been launched for a seven-year period 
beginning 2005-06. In the area of health, the Natio nal Rural Health Mission 
(NRHM) has been set up with the objective of provid ing accessible, 
affordable, accountable and effective health care d elivery especially to the 
poor and the vulnerable sections of the society and  bridge gaps in health care. 
In education, the Sarva Siksha Abhiyan (SSA) is being implemented to provide 
elementary education to ail children in the 6—14 ye ars age group. For global 
integration of the Indian economy, there has been a progressive reduction in the 
tariff rates. The Budget for 2007-08 has proposed r eduction in the peak 
customs tariff rate to 10%. A Committee on Infrastr ucture has been set up 
under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister with the o bjective of initiating 
policies that ensure time-

Salient features of UIDSSMT  
Urban Infrastructure Development Scheme for Small &  Medium Towns 
(UIDSSMT) aim at improvement in urban infrastructure in towns and cities (other 
than the 63 cities identified under JNNURM) in a planned manner. It subsumes 
the existing schemes viz. Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns 
(IDSMT) and Accelerated Urban Water Supply Programm e (AUWSP). The 
scheme will apply to all cities/towns as per 2001 c ensus, excepting 
cities/towns covered under Jawaharlal Nehru Nationa l Urban Renewal 
Mission (JNNURM). 
Objectives: 
a) Improve infrastructure! facilities and help create durable public assets and 
quality oriented services in cities and towns, 
b) Enhance public-private-partnership in infrastructure! development and 
c) Promote planned integrated development of towns and cities. 
Components: 
The components for assistance under the scheme will  include all urban 
infrastructure development projects including water supply and sewerage. The 
scheme will cover the following areas: 
• Urban Renewal 
• Water supply & sanitation 
199 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
• Sewerage and solid waste management 
• Construction and improvement of drains/storm water drains 
• Construction/upgradation of roads, highways/expressways 
• Parking lots/spaces on public private partnership basis 
• Development of heritage areas 
• Prevention and rehabilitation of soil erosion/land slides 
Financing Pattern 
 
• The sharing of funds would be in the ration of 80:1 0 between Central 
Government and State Government and balance 10% could be raised by the 
nodal agencies from Financial Institutions. 
• Central Assistance (Grant) is released directly to the nodal agencies as 
Additional Central Assistance (ACA). 
• Central share is released in two instalments depending on availability of State 
share and submission of Utilisation Certificate within 12 months of the 
closure of the-financial year. 
Reforms 
The provision of Central assistance is linked to im plementation of certain 
mandatory as well as optional reforms at the State and ULB/Para-Statal levels. 
Implementation of all manadotry and optional reform s has to be completed 
during the Mission period.

Development of slum areas in Delhi  
2706. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Ministe r of 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made plans to involve private builders in the 
development of sprawling slum areas in Delhi and to  rehabilitate the shanty 
dwellers; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI AJAY MAKEN): (a) and (b) Master P lan of Delhi 
(MPD)-2021 provides for an alternate approach for r ehabilitation/relocation of 
slum and J J clusters. Broadly speaking, the alternate approach should have the 
following components: 
(i) Resettlement, whether in the form of in-situ up-gradation or relocation, should 
be based mainly on built up accommodation of around  23 sqm with 
common areas and facilities, rather than on the mod el of horizontal 
plotted development. 
(ii) The concept of land as a resource should be ad opted to develop such 
accommodation with private sector participation and  investment, to 
the extent possible. However, the subject of rehabi litation of J J 
dwellers mainly pertains to Slum/JJ Wing of MCD/Lan d Owning 
agency. ' 
(iii) Incentives by way of higher FAR, part commercial use of the land and, 
if necessary and feasible, Transfer of Development Rights should be 
provided. 
(iv) A cooperative resettlement model with adequate  safeguards may be 
adopted with tenure rights being provided through the institution of Co-
operative Societies. 
(v) The provision of accommodation should be based on cost with suitable 
arrangements for funding/financing, keepingjn view the aspect of 
affordability and capacity to pay. 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [26 April, 2007] 
(vi) In cases of relocation, the sites should be id entified with a view to 
develop relatively small clusters in a manner that they can be 
integrated with the overall planned development of the area, 
particularly keeping in view the availability of employment avenues in the 
vicinity. Very large resettlement sites could lead to a phenomenon of 
planned slums. 
(vii) Suitable arrangement for temporary transit accommodation for families 
to be rehabilitated should be made. This may preferably be near or at the 
same site and the utilization of these may be synch ronized with the 
phases of implementation of the scheme of io-situ up-gradation. 
(viii) Community Based Organisations (CBOs) and Non -Governmental 
Organisations (NGOs) should be closely involved in the resettlement 
process.

 †2711. SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRI SATYAVRAT CHATURVEDI: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a number of companies in NCR are collecting funds 
from the investors in the name of prelaunching even without having land; 
tb) if so, the number of complaints received by Gov ernment against such 
companies so far; and 
(c) the action taken by Government to protect such investors from 
cheating and to get their money refunded? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI AJAY MAKEN) (a) to (c) The Nation al Capital 
Region Planning Board (NCRPB) has informed that it does not allocate land to 
agencies/companies for development purposes and this function is performed 
by State Governments, Urban local bodies, development authorities, viz. Delhi 
Development Authority (DDA), Haryana Urban Developm ent Authority 
(HUDA), Ghaziabad Development Authority (GDA) etc. and other parastatals. 
The Ghaziabad Development Authority, Hapur-Pilkhuwa Development 
Authority and Meerut Development Authority have informed that on the. basis 
of certain complaints of illegal pre-launching of Housing/Commercial schemes by 
private builders, the authorities have issued public notices advising people not 
to get misled by such advertisements.

PPP model for creation of sports infrastructure  
2719. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state whether his Ministry has 
any plans to create a private-public partnership mo del for creation of 
sports infrastructure like stadia etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI  
SHANKAR AIYAR): There are two existing schemes that  focus oh the 
Private-Public Partnership mode for the development of sports infrastructure in the 
country viz., the National Sports Development Fund Scheme and the  State 
Sports Academy Scheme. Under the National Sports De velopment Fund 
Scheme, there is a provision to accept contribution s from different entities, 
including corporates. On receipt of such contributi ons, the Government also 
contributes on a matching basis for augmenting the corpus. However, there has 
been negligible contribution by the corporate sector to NSDF. The objects of 
the fund include creation of sports infrastructure.  The State Sports Academy 
Scheme involves a financing pattern in the ratio of 51:25:24 between the Private 
sponsor, the Central Government and the State Gover nment. The Central 
Government contribution is restricted to 25% of the  capital cost subject to a 
ceiling of Rs. 218 lakhs; and 25% of the recurring Gosts subject to a maximum 
of Rs. 17 lakhs per annum for a period of 3 years. The cost of the land is not 
included in the scheme and is required to be provid ed gratis by the State 
Government or the sponsor. So, far, Ministry has not received any proposal for State 
Sports Academy with private sector/corporate sector participation.
